claims.text: Curtailing atomic mobility during nanoparticle reduction favors stochastic incorporation of multiple elemental species.
Restricted atomic mobility governs the formation of single-phase homogeneous noble metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
The initial system contains multiple noble metal precursors.
The noble metal precursors may be provided in a single-source formulation.
The initial precursors are unsintered and spatially distributed within a support or solid matrix.
Low-temperature reduction can be used to restrict precursor mobility.
Rapid quenching restricts the free mobility of metal precursors.
Immobilizing supports or environments restrict the free mobility of metal precursors.
Immobilized low- to moderate-temperature conditions ensure rapid reduction and immediate kinetic trapping of the atoms.
A support or solid precursor framework mediates the limitation of atomic mobility.
Limited atomic mobility promotes stochastic mixing and prevents elemental segregation.
Each reduced metal atom is trapped before it can diffuse and cluster with like atoms.
Restricted mobility produces statistically random incorporation of all constituent metals into a uniform lattice.
Freely mobile atoms may segregate and produce phase separation.
Restricted-mobility conditions should yield nanoparticles with a single homogeneous phase and nearly uniform elemental distribution.
Higher-mobility conditions should yield phase-separated or elementally segregated nanoparticles.
Unconstrained precursor mobility causes sequential reduction, clustering, phase segregation, or uncontrolled morphology.
The hypothesis applies to low-temperature noble metal systems containing at least five elements.
The hypothesis may not apply to high-temperature routes or methods with inherently high precursor mobility.
The quantitative contribution of mobility restriction relative to reduction kinetics and precursor chemistry is not fully characterized and may be system-dependent.
